passage:
"I keep hearing it, Aparna-didi. Nani said, 'Come when your exams finish, no hurry.' And I said, 'Next month, promise.'"
Aparna set down the steel tumblers. "Rukmini, that's the fourth time this week you've told me about that call."
"Because if I'd taken the Friday bus instead of waiting for results, I'd have seen her. I'd have noticed she was breathless. I'd have—"
"You'd have what? Stopped her heart from doing what it did?"
Rukmini twisted her dupatta around her fingers. "At least then it would properly be my fault. Now it's just... nothing I can hold."
Aparna sat beside her on the divan. "Amma says the same about not calling the doctor that Sunday. Three months, and you two keep taking turns blaming yourselves."
"So what do I do with it?"
"Say it to me instead of to the ceiling at two in the morning. And maybe you try the counselling centre at your college. I'll come with you the first time."

qa.q: What did Rukmini promise Nani on their last phone call?
qa.a: Rukmini said, 'Next month, promise,' after Nani told her to come when her exams finished.

qa.q: Why might Rukmini wish the death were 'properly' her fault?
qa.a: Blaming herself gives her something to hold on to; guilt feels easier than accepting that Nani's death was never in her hands.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Rukmini at this stage?
qa.a: She can say the what-ifs out loud to Aparna instead of looping alone at night, and take up the offer to visit the college counselling centre together.

qa.q: How is Aparna affected as she listens to her sister?
qa.a: Aparna is grieving Nani too, and she is watching both Amma and Rukmini blame themselves, so she is trying to steady the family while carrying her own loss.

grounding: Shows a young adult replaying the last phone call and clinging to self-blame as a false sense of control months after a death.

passage:
My name is Kamal, and for most of last winter I lived inside a four-minute phone call. Dadu rang on a Tuesday to ask whether the Pune rains had stopped. I was late for a birthday dinner, so I said, "I'll call you Sunday, I'm coming home in December anyway." He died on Thursday.
For months I rebuilt that call. If I had stayed on longer. If I had booked the October train. If I had heard something in his cough. Every version ended with me catching it in time and getting him to a hospital.
Looking back, those what-ifs were oddly comforting, like I still had my hands on a steering wheel. Rukmini, my lab partner, finally asked me one evening, "Would the doctors in Guwahati have done anything different because you were in the room?" I didn't have an answer. That was the first night in weeks I slept straight through.

qa.q: How long was Kamal's last phone call with Dadu?
qa.a: It was a four-minute phone call.

qa.q: Why did the what-ifs feel 'oddly comforting' to Kamal?
qa.a: Every imagined version ended with Kamal catching the illness in time, so the guilt gave a feeling of still having hands on a steering wheel.

qa.q: What helped Kamal step out of the loop, and what else could help if it came back?
qa.a: Rukmini's plain question about whether being in the room would have changed anything loosened it; if the loop returns, talking it through with a friend or a college counsellor could help.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt before asking that question?
qa.a: Rukmini may have been unsure how to help a grieving lab partner, and chose a calm, factual question rather than simply saying 'don't blame yourself'.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult looping on what-ifs about a last call and how that guilt felt like control over a death that was out of reach.

passage:
In her Bengaluru hostel room, Keerthana lay awake again, replaying the last call with Ammamma. It had been four months.
"Come for Pongal, kanna," Ammamma had said. "I'll make your sweet pongal."
"Next month, promise. Exams."
Next month never came.
If only she had taken the bus that weekend. If only she'd noticed that Ammamma's voice sounded tired. If only, if only. Every night the call played, and every night she changed her answer.
Siddharth, her friend from the next wing, found her on the steps one morning. "Keerthu, you couldn't have known. The doctors didn't know."
"But if I'd gone..."
"It still wouldn't have been in your hands." She stared at her shoes and didn't answer.

qa.q: What did Ammamma say she would make for Keerthana?
qa.a: Sweet pongal.

qa.q: What is Keerthana feeling as she replays the call each night?
qa.a: She feels guilty and grieving, imagining that a different answer could have changed what happened.

qa.q: What turning point could help Keerthana out of the loop?
qa.a: Hearing, perhaps from a counsellor as well as Siddharth, that the death was never in her hands, and grieving without the what-ifs.

qa.q: What is Siddharth experiencing as he tries to reassure her?
qa.a: He seems concerned and a little helpless, wanting to lift her guilt but seeing she can't accept it yet.

grounding: Shows a young woman replaying her grandmother's last call and blaming herself for not visiting sooner, a guilt that loops for months.

passage:
"Joseph, can I ask you something?"
"Always, Maria."
"Papa called me that Saturday. I was at the mall with friends. I said, 'I'll call you back tomorrow, Papa.'"
"I know."
"If I'd stayed on the phone. If I'd heard something in his voice. If I'd gone home that weekend..."
"Maria."
"I keep thinking I could have made him see a doctor."
"He didn't tell any of us he was feeling unwell. Not Mummy, not me."
"But I was his favourite. He'd have told me."
Joseph put his arm around her. "You're looking for a door that was never there."
Maria cried into his shoulder, still whispering, "If only."

qa.q: Where was Maria when Papa called that Saturday?
qa.a: At the mall with friends.

qa.q: What does Maria's belief that Papa would have told her suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She feels deep guilt and a need for control, as if she could have prevented his death if she had listened.

qa.q: What could help Maria at this stage of her grief?
qa.a: Hearing again, patiently, that the death was not in her hands, and perhaps talking with a counsellor about the looping guilt.

qa.q: What is it like for Joseph to hear Maria's what-ifs?
qa.a: Joseph is grieving too and probably sad and protective, trying gently to free her from blame.

grounding: Shows a young woman replaying her father's last call and imagining she could have saved him, a guilt that gives false control.

passage:
It's been six months since Dida died, and I still replay that call. She rang on a Wednesday. I was in the library. I whispered, "Dida, I'll call you on Sunday." She said, "Okay, shona, eat well."
She died on Friday.
Looking back, I've built a hundred other Wednesdays. In one, I take the train home. In another, I hear her cough and phone the doctor. In every one, I save her. My sister Kashish says, "Arnab, she was eighty-seven. Her heart was tired." I know that. But the what-ifs feel better than helplessness, somehow. At least in them I could have done something.
I think I'll talk to the college counsellor next week. The loop is getting old.

qa.q: When did Dida die?
qa.a: She died on Friday.

qa.q: Why do the what-ifs feel better to Arnab than helplessness?
qa.a: Arnab's guilt gives a feeling of control, as if the death could have been stopped, which hurts less than feeling powerless.

qa.q: What turning point does Arnab reach at the end?
qa.a: Deciding to see the college counsellor, recognising the loop of what-ifs has lasted too long.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel hearing Arnab's self-blame?
qa.a: Kashish is probably sad and worried, trying to remind Arnab that Dida's tired heart was nobody's fault.

grounding: Shows a young adult replaying a grandmother's last call for months, guilt giving an illusion of control, and deciding to seek counselling.

passage:
College counselling centre, session note, Wednesday.
Mohit's roommate, Hrithik, walked him to my door this morning and waited outside. Mohit's Dadaji died in Kanpur four months ago. Mohit keeps replaying their last phone call: Dadaji asked when he was coming home, and Mohit said, "After exams, pakka." Dadaji died two weeks before exams ended. Today Mohit said "if only" nine times. If only he had taken the train in October. If only he had skipped the fest. I asked what he could actually have known in October. He said, very quietly, "Nothing. He sounded fine." We talked about how guilt can feel easier than helplessness, because guilt pretends we had control. He cried for the first time in our sessions. Next session is booked for Monday. Hrithik has the centre's number and knows to call if Mohit seems worse before then.

qa.q: How many times did Mohit say "if only" today?
qa.a: Mohit said "if only" nine times.

qa.q: Why might Mohit keep replaying the last phone call?
qa.a: He feels guilty and helpless; blaming himself gives him a sense of control over a death he could not have prevented.

qa.q: What turning point does the counsellor offer at this stage?
qa.a: The counsellor asks what Mohit could really have known in October, helping him see that the guilt pretends he had control, and books another session.

qa.q: What might it be like for Hrithik to walk Mohit to the centre?
qa.a: Hrithik is probably worried and protective, waiting outside and staying ready to call the centre if Mohit seems worse.

grounding: Shows a young adult looping on the last phone call and what-ifs, with guilt standing in for control over a death that was never in his hands.
